title: Polynomial-time stable matching in unimodular hypergraphs
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
formal: Is there one deterministic algorithm and constants \(C>0\), \(k\ge1\) as below that, for every explicitly given finite hypergraph with totally unimodular incidence matrix and strict vertex preferences, returns a stable matching in at most \(C(L+1)^k\) steps, where \(L\) is the full input bit length?
why: Tests whether a strong integrality promise can turn guaranteed coalition stability into an efficient algorithm. It extends the computational perspective of classical stable matching while keeping the target independent of optimization over stable outcomes.
status_note: Rechecked on 13 September 2026. The ICALP 2025 source leaves general unimodular stable matching open. Chandrasekaran–Kalathur’s August 2026 preprint gives a polynomial-time algorithm for network hypergraphs, a subclass. No general resolution was located in the bounded subsequent-work check; the new proof was not independently audited.

references.title: Stable Hypergraph Matching in Unimodular Hypergraphs
references.authors: Biró, Péter; Csáji, Gergely; Schlotter, Ildikó
references.locator: Unresolved-question passage on page 19; PDF page 19

definitions: The input explicitly lists vertices \(V=[n]\), \(n\ge0\), distinct nonempty hyperedges \(E=\{e_1,\ldots,e_m\}\subseteq2^V\), and, for each vertex, a permutation of its incident edge indices from most to least preferred. Vertex and edge indices are binary encoded with ordinary length-delimited list syntax; the input length \(L\) counts every listed vertex, incidence and preference entry. The incidence matrix is \(A_{v,j}=1\) for \(v\in e_j\) and zero otherwise. The promise is total unimodularity: every square submatrix has determinant in \(\{-1,0,1\}\). A matching \(M\subseteq E\) consists of pairwise disjoint edges. Every vertex prefers any incident edge to remaining unmatched. An edge \(e\notin M\) blocks \(M\) if every \(v\in e\) is unmatched or strictly prefers \(e\) to the unique edge of \(M\) containing \(v\). Stability means no edge blocks. There are no ties, capacities above one, edge-size bounds or optimization objective. Use one deterministic multitape Turing machine, without advice, randomness or an oracle, running within \(C(L+1)^k\) steps for fixed \(C>0\) and integer \(k\ge1\) on every input string. It must return a list of edge indices forming a stable matching on every well-formed promised instance; its answer outside that promise is unrestricted.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a uniform polynomial-time algorithm satisfying the stated search specification on all promised instances, or prove in Lean that no such algorithm exists. A conditional complexity lower bound establishes only its conditional conclusion. Fractional existence, finding a stable solution in a proper subclass, and optimizing the weight of a stable solution are distinct targets.

context_blocks.title: Coalitions rather than pairs
context_blocks.text: A hyperedge represents a group that could cooperate. Selected groups cannot share members. Stability forbids an unselected group whose members would all prefer forming it to their current situation. The input includes each participant’s ranking, so merely finding disjoint groups is insufficient.

context_blocks.title: Existence and computation
context_blocks.text: The source explains why total unimodularity together with a classical stable-fractional existence theorem guarantees an integral stable matching. It does not give a general polynomial running-time bound. Hardness of maximizing weight among stable matchings is a different question from finding any stable one.

context_blocks.title: A newer special-case result
context_blocks.text: An August 2026 preprint gives a polynomial-time algorithm for network hypergraphs. In that class the ground elements are arcs of an oriented tree and each hyperedge is a directed tree path. Network hypergraphs are a subclass of unimodular hypergraphs, so this narrows the open frontier without resolving the general target.

Without a structural promise, stability can fail even for groups of size two. On three vertices with possible pairs ab, bc and ca, let a prefer ab to ca, b prefer bc to ab, and c prefer ca to bc. Every chosen pair is blocked by another pair, and the empty matching is blocked as well. The incidence matrix of this triangle has a square determinant of magnitude two, so it is outside the totally unimodular domain.

The objective is to return any stable matching. Different vertices may favor different stable outcomes, but the card imposes no social-welfare, maximum-cardinality, or weighted objective. This distinction matters because optimizing over stable outcomes can be hard even in a class where finding one outcome is efficient.
